analysis.one_liner: Bans brand-name drug makers from paying generic competitors to delay launching cheaper drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House Energy and Commerce Committee by voice vote in April 2019 and was placed on the House calendar that May, but it never received a floor vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Drug companies sometimes settle patent lawsuits by paying a generic or biosimilar maker to stay off the market for years — a practice known as 'pay for delay.' This bill makes those payments unlawful, with civil penalties set by the Federal Trade Commission and loss of the first-to-file generic's special exclusivity period. It also requires company executives to certify under oath that everything they file about a settlement is complete, including side agreements and oral promises. If it had passed, cheaper versions of drugs would reach patients sooner.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay out of pocket for prescriptions, and anyone with insurance premiums or taxes tied to drug prices, because brand-name monopolies would end sooner and cheaper generics and biosimilars would enter the market faster.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and anyone paying for prescriptions

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits agreements in which a brand-name drug maker gives anything of value to a generic or biosimilar maker in exchange for delaying or giving up research, manufacturing, marketing, or sales of the competing product [S2] [S3] [S4].
Lets the FTC enforce the ban as an unfair or deceptive practice, with civil penalties up to three times the value of the deal, plus injunctions [S2] [S3] [S4].
Strips the 180-day exclusivity period from any first-to-file generic maker that enters a prohibited delay agreement, removing the incentive for those deals [S2] [S3] [S4].

Requires the CEO or lead negotiator to certify that the agreements filed with the FTC and Justice Department are complete, including ancillary and oral agreements — closing a loophole where side deals were never disclosed [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name and biologic drug makers, which would lose the ability to extend monopolies by paying competitors to stay out of the market; generic makers would lose lucrative settlement payments but could enter the market sooner.

drawbacks.text: Generic and biosimilar makers lose a real revenue stream: settlement payments from brand companies, which some manufacturers used to fund operations; the bill assumes earlier market entry compensates for that [S2] [S4].
The FTC has exclusive power to enforce the ban, so consumers and competitors could not sue on their own, leaving enforcement dependent on one agency's priorities and staffing [S2] [S3].

The bill leaves room for settlements it deems legitimate — including early-entry licenses, covenants not to sue, and up to $7.5 million in litigation costs — and lets the FTC exempt other agreements it finds pro-competitive, so some delay deals could survive [S4].
It applies only to agreements signed after enactment, so any deals already made would continue [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — faster access to cheaper generic and biosimilar versions of drugs — goes directly to patients and health budgets, while the cost falls on brand-name manufacturers and partly on generic makers' settlement income. The strongest honest objection is that enforcement rests entirely with the FTC and that carve-outs leave some deals legal. But the core prohibition is straightforward, and the bill amends rather than replaces existing antitrust law [S4].

outcome.mechanism: It cleared committee and was placed on the House calendar in May 2019, but House leaders never scheduled a floor vote, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2021 [S6].

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush introduced the bill on March 5, 2019, targeting settlements in which a brand-name drug maker pays a generic or biosimilar maker to stay off the market [S1] [S2].

The House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health forwarded an amended version to the full committee by voice vote in March 2019, and the full committee ordered it reported by voice vote in April 2019 [S6].

On May 10, 2019, the committee formally reported the bill (House Report 116-52), the Judiciary Committee was discharged, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar — the House's list of bills awaiting floor action [S3] [S6].
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a House floor vote and expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S6] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: with no vote ever held, they kept the option of paying generic and biosimilar competitors to delay entry, and higher-priced monopolies continued longer than the bill would have allowed. Patients did not get the earlier competition the bill promised.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote after it was placed on the Union Calendar in May 2019, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress [S6].

sides.party_line_note: All 39 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on, though the committee reported the bill on a voice vote with no recorded dissent [S5] [S6].

industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful to pay generic or biosimilar makers to delay market entry, with penalties up to three times the deal's value. Those delay payments are what extend brand-name monopolies and keep drug prices high, so the industry's interest runs directly against patients here.

Generic makers lose the settlement payments that brand companies offered them, but they gain the right to launch earlier without agreed-upon delays — and a first-to-file generic that signs a delay deal would forfeit its valuable 180-day exclusivity period. Their core business of selling cheaper competing drugs benefits from the ban.
The bill gives the FTC exclusive enforcement authority over these agreements, including civil penalty actions and cease-and-desist orders.
